proposedOverrides.name: Alsea people
proposedOverrides.summary: The Alsea are an Indigenous people of the central Oregon coast, including the Alsea River and Cape Perpetua area. Their history includes coastal food gathering, language and storytelling, forced displacement and continuing community life.

scopeNotes: The imported polygon covers 1492 to 1500 in the central Oregon coastal region. Its endpoints are not founding or extinction dates. The Alsea people are distinct from the modern town, the reservation administration and other peoples confined at the Alsea Subagency. The imported boundary remains unverified.

The earliest dated institutional phase begins with the 1855 Coast Reservation, not the beginning of Alsea occupation. Undated household practices are not given invented fifteenth-century dates merely to fill the selected-year view.

Drucker’s pages 81 and 85 and title-page information were read in indexed extracts after the library download returned an empty file. His introduction’s disparagement of Alsea culture and prediction that nothing important would happen are rejected. Ludson and Albert are named as knowledge contributors, and their memories are not presented as archaeological observations.

Drucker reports a disagreement between Ludson and Albert over disposal of fish entrails. The disputed detail and sweeping claims about food preferences are omitted. No unsupported anatomical dimensions or exact ancient construction date is assigned to remembered houses.

Frachtenberg’s introduction on pages 9 to 10 was read in indexed text; the complete Smithsonian PDF could not be downloaded. The book’s contributors and editorial methods are used, not unread stories or the author’s assertion that his collection exhausts surviving knowledge. His judgments of speakers’ reliability are not adopted.

The Smithsonian sound-recording description was read in the indexed finding aid, page 636. NAA INV.00000550 identifies the exact disc. The audio was not auditioned, and no performance details or new translation are inferred. Catalog regional labels are not used to move the Alsea homeland inland.

Whereat Phillips’s name discussion is her documented research with Buckley, not a certain etymology. Hanis and Lower Umpqua versions are distinguished from the Alsea name, and cross-community transmission is not treated as identity of the languages.

Lewis’s article presents original archival transcriptions and an interpretation of removal timing. Jack Rogers is explicitly Coos, not relabeled Alsea. Collective administrative labels can include several peoples. Apparent consent in agents’ reports is not treated as proof of free choice, and a 1875 order is distinct from a later movement.

The Siletz comprehensive-plan history explicitly lists Alsea/Yaquina among constituent peoples. Its acreage totals and other numerical generalizations are not repeated. The current tribal welcome verifies continuing government and distinguishes the 1954 law from its effect in 1956.

Public Law 95-195 section 3 was read in indexed text. The narrative describes historical recognition and service eligibility, not current hunting or fishing law, land title, membership eligibility or an automatic restoration of all territory.
Independent historical review, border assessment and depth certification remain pending.
